  - Against: Fixing the instructions did not always hold: the Pokémon port's agent kept hard-coding behaviour after being told not to ([Pokémon](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-01-25-vjeux-pokemon-showdown-rust.md#what-went-wrong)), and 1Password's ordering errors persisted under explicit rules ([1Password](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-04-20-1password-monolith-refactor.md#what-went-wrong)).
- **KNW-2** [stated] Stamp each unit with its status, tune against the largest failing group using a small sample, then sweep all units again.
  - Old system as oracle: partly. Depends on model ability: no. Strength: strong. Era: 2024–2026; newest: Gemini (internal).
  - Cases: [Airbnb: what worked](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-04-01-airbnb-enzyme-to-rtl.md#what-worked), [Slack: what worked](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2024-05-22-slack-enzyme-to-rtl.md#what-worked), [Google: what worked](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-04-13-google-int64-ids.md#what-worked), [Uber: what worked](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-04-07-uber-junit4-to-junit5.md#what-worked).
  - Against: None found.
- **KNW-3** [stated] Keep structured session logs from the start; they later answered where time went and what people did, and became evaluations.
  - Old system as oracle: no. Depends on model ability: no. Strength: medium. Era: 2026; newest: Claude Opus 5.x.
  - Cases: [GitHub: numbers](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-09-16-github-copilot-runtime-rust.md#numbers), [GitHub: what worked](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-09-16-github-copilot-runtime-rust.md#what-worked).
  - Against: GitHub's split of the engineer's messages by intent was labelled by an LLM, not checked by a person ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-09-16-github-copilot-runtime-rust.md#numbers)).
- **KNW-4** [stated] A compacted or fresh session forgets what the last one learned; keep the method in files it rereads (instructions, one debug script) and find work by search.
  - Old system as oracle: no. Depends on model ability: partly. Strength: medium. Era: 2025–2026; newest: Claude (version unstated).
  - Cases: [Pokémon: what went wrong](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-01-25-vjeux-pokemon-showdown-rust.md#what-went-wrong), [Pokémon: what worked](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-01-25-vjeux-pokemon-showdown-rust.md#what-worked), [Datadog: what worked](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-06-23-datadog-foundationdb-to-postgres.md#what-worked).
  - Against: The gains are unmeasured: PagerDuty's author credits a growing file of fix patterns with faster fixes later in the run and in the next upgrade ([PagerDuty](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-04-13-pagerduty-rundeck-grails-7.md#what-worked)), and the Pokémon account gives no measure of time saved, and a search finds only the markers the agent wrote, not stubs it left unmarked ([Pokémon](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-01-25-vjeux-pokemon-showdown-rust.md#what-worked)); such files also go stale: at Temporal a migration left an agent guide pointing at deleted code, and nothing flagged it ([Temporal](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-09-02-temporal-billing-store-clickhouse.md#what-went-wrong)).
- **KNW-5** [stated] Mark temporary migration code the day you write it with what it is for and how to remove it; an agent can later find the notes and work through them as the removal list.
  - Old system as oracle: no. Depends on model ability: partly. Strength: weak. Era: 2026; newest: unstated.
  - Cases: [Temporal: what worked](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-09-02-temporal-billing-store-clickhouse.md#what-worked).
  - Against: None found; one team's account, its prompt record misses the early weeks, and it gives no count of leftovers the notes did not cover ([Temporal](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-09-02-temporal-billing-store-clickhouse.md#what-went-wrong)).

## Measuring and reading results (measurement.md)

How to read the numbers in these sources, and how to report your own.

- **MSR-1** [ours] Treat savings measured against a manual effort that never ran as self-estimates; record the basis beside each figure and never add them across cases.
  - Old system as oracle: no. Depends on model ability: no. Strength: strong. Era: 2024–2026; newest: Claude Fable 5.x.
  - Cases: [Google: what went wrong](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-04-13-google-int64-ids.md#what-went-wrong), [Spotify: numbers](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-11-06-spotify-honk.md#numbers), [Airbnb: numbers](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-04-01-airbnb-enzyme-to-rtl.md#numbers), [Slack: numbers](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2024-05-22-slack-enzyme-to-rtl.md#numbers), [Bun: numbers](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-07-08-bun-zig-to-rust.md#numbers), [1Password: what went wrong](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-04-20-1password-monolith-refactor.md#what-went-wrong), [PagerDuty: numbers](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-04-13-pagerduty-rundeck-grails-7.md#numbers), [Mindstone: numbers](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-07-06-mindstone-go-to-typescript.md#numbers).
  - Against: Google's estimate at least agrees with its measured shares of model-made edits ([Google](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-04-13-google-int64-ids.md#numbers)).
- **MSR-2** [ours] For every success rate ask out of what (attempted, opened, merged, dropped from scope), and report each measure with its base; bases differed several-fold.
  - Old system as oracle: no. Depends on model ability: no. Strength: strong. Era: 2024–2026; newest: Claude Opus 4.x.
  - Cases: [Spotify: what went wrong](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-11-06-spotify-honk.md#what-went-wrong), [Slack: how it was checked](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2024-05-22-slack-enzyme-to-rtl.md#how-it-was-checked), [Zalando: how it was checked](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-02-20-zalando-ui-component-libraries.md#how-it-was-checked), [Bloomberg: how it was checked](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-11-03-bloomberg-python-cpp-uplift.md#how-it-was-checked), [Spartacus: what went wrong](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-04-13-lutz-leonhardt-spartacus-signal-forms.md#what-went-wrong).
  - Against: Airbnb's main rate covers its whole file set ([Airbnb](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-04-01-airbnb-enzyme-to-rtl.md#numbers)).
- **MSR-3** [ours] Weigh each source by the author's stake in the tool (seller, owner, partner); none of the cases had outside measurement.
  - Old system as oracle: no. Depends on model ability: no. Strength: medium. Era: 2025–2026; newest: Claude Opus 5.x.
  - Cases: [Bun: who did what](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-07-08-bun-zig-to-rust.md#who-did-what), [GitHub: context](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-09-16-github-copilot-runtime-rust.md#context), [Spotify: context](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-11-06-spotify-honk.md#context), [1Password: context](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-04-20-1password-monolith-refactor.md#context), [Intel: who did what](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-08-24-intel-ideas-c-to-rust.md#who-did-what).
  - Against: Google lists its own threats to validity ([Google](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-04-13-google-int64-ids.md#what-went-wrong)), and Slack has no stake in the model it used ([Slack](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2024-05-22-slack-enzyme-to-rtl.md#who-did-what)).
- **MSR-4** [stated] Credit a gain to the migration only after separating it from work that landed in the same window (other speed work, linker changes, unrelated fixes).
  - Old system as oracle: partly. Depends on model ability: no. Strength: medium. Era: 2026; newest: Claude Opus 5.x.
  - Cases: [GitHub: what went wrong](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-09-16-github-copilot-runtime-rust.md#what-went-wrong), [Bun: what went wrong](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-07-08-bun-zig-to-rust.md#what-went-wrong).
  - Against: Disagree: the Zig creator credits link-time optimisation the old toolchain already had for Bun's speed-up ([Bun](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-07-08-bun-zig-to-rust.md#what-went-wrong)).
- **MSR-5** [stated] Escaped defects are unknown by nature: publish known regressions as a floor, grouped by cause, and use a before-and-after proxy labelled as a proxy.
  - Old system as oracle: partly. Depends on model ability: no. Strength: medium. Era: 2026; newest: Claude Opus 5.x.
  - Cases: [GitHub: what went wrong](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-09-16-github-copilot-runtime-rust.md#what-went-wrong), [Bun: what went wrong](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-07-08-bun-zig-to-rust.md#what-went-wrong).
  - Against: Airbnb reports no defects after merge at all, which is missing data, not evidence ([Airbnb](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-04-01-airbnb-enzyme-to-rtl.md#what-went-wrong)).
- **MSR-6** [ours] Activity numbers (lines per minute, commits, merged changes) are not progress; track verified behaviour or the shrinking list of remaining sites.
  - Old system as oracle: partly. Depends on model ability: no. Strength: medium. Era: 2025–2026; newest: GPT-6.x.
  - Cases: [Bun: numbers](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-07-08-bun-zig-to-rust.md#numbers), [Spotify: numbers](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-11-06-spotify-honk.md#numbers), [GitHub: what went wrong](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-09-16-github-copilot-runtime-rust.md#what-went-wrong), [Pokémon: how it was checked](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-01-25-vjeux-pokemon-showdown-rust.md#how-it-was-checked), [ts-rust: what went wrong](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-10-07-ping-tsgo-to-rust.md#what-went-wrong).
  - Against: None found.
- **MSR-7** [ours] Re-date a lesson before reusing it: early negative results, and results from pre-release or restricted models, may not hold for the models you use.
  - Old system as oracle: no. Depends on model ability: partly. Strength: medium. Era: 2024–2026; newest: GPT-5.x.
  - Cases: [Slack: who did what](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2024-05-22-slack-enzyme-to-rtl.md#who-did-what), [Bun: who did what](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-07-08-bun-zig-to-rust.md#who-did-what), [Intel: who did what](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-08-24-intel-ideas-c-to-rust.md#who-did-what), [Google: what went wrong](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-04-13-google-int64-ids.md#what-went-wrong), [Uber: what went wrong](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-04-07-uber-junit4-to-junit5.md#what-went-wrong).
  - Against: 1Password's 2026 agents still broke ordering rules ([1Password](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-04-20-1password-monolith-refactor.md#what-went-wrong)), so some failures persist across eras.
- **MSR-8** [ours] Do not credit the model with work the deterministic tools did: finding sites, building manifests and codemods were often the hard part.
  - Old system as oracle: no. Depends on model ability: no. Strength: strong. Era: 2024–2026; newest: Claude Opus 4.x.
  - Cases: [Google: who did what](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-04-13-google-int64-ids.md#who-did-what), [Slack: who did what](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2024-05-22-slack-enzyme-to-rtl.md#who-did-what), [1Password: who did what](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-04-20-1password-monolith-refactor.md#who-did-what), [Spotify: who did what](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-11-06-spotify-honk.md#who-did-what), [Uber: who did what](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-04-07-uber-junit4-to-junit5.md#who-did-what), [Bloomberg: who did what](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-11-03-bloomberg-python-cpp-uplift.md#who-did-what).
  - Against: In Bun almost all the work ran through agent workflows ([Bun](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-07-08-bun-zig-to-rust.md#who-did-what)).
- **MSR-9** [stated] If you will claim savings, measure people's share from file snapshots or logs from day one; estimates from the tool's own builders are biased.
  - Old system as oracle: no. Depends on model ability: no. Strength: medium. Era: 2025–2026; newest: Gemini (internal).
  - Cases: [Google: how it was checked](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-04-13-google-int64-ids.md#how-it-was-checked), [Google: what went wrong](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-04-13-google-int64-ids.md#what-went-wrong), [Temporal: what went wrong](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-09-02-temporal-billing-store-clickhouse.md#what-went-wrong).
  - Against: Google itself warns that edit distance misses the thinking behind edits, and the snapshot method skips edits made along the way, so it understates people's share ([Google](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-04-13-google-int64-ids.md#what-went-wrong)).
- **MSR-10** [stated] A merge rate undercounts unrequested changes: also count targets whose owners rejected the change and then migrated anyway, often reusing it.
  - Old system as oracle: no. Depends on model ability: no. Strength: weak. Era: 2025–2026; newest: Claude Opus 4.x.
  - Cases: [Bloomberg: what worked](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-11-03-bloomberg-python-cpp-uplift.md#what-worked).
  - Against: None found; Bloomberg followed up only the rejected Python PRs, not the far larger group left without a decision ([Bloomberg](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-11-03-bloomberg-python-cpp-uplift.md#what-worked)).

## Cases

- [Bloomberg opens 2,333 migration PRs for Python packaging and C++ builds with a hybrid pipeline](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-11-03-bloomberg-python-cpp-uplift.md) — mixed, an in-house shared-environment Python packaging model; CppBuild, an in-house C++ build system to PyPackaging, an in-house per-package dependency model; CMake; AI share: unstated; evidence: shown-in-source; author: user-of-tool; cost: unstated. A rule-driven pipeline with Claude in bounded steps opened 2,333 packaging and build PRs; 729 were merged, and most got no decision from their owners.
- [Ping.gg ports the Go TypeScript 7 compiler to Rust with coding agents, after a restart](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-10-07-ping-tsgo-to-rust.md) — language, Go (TypeScript 7 native compiler, type checker, language server and API) to Rust (tsc-rs); AI share: most; evidence: assertion-only; author: user-of-tool; cost: over $420,000 in API-priced tokens in all (over $400,000 first attempts, ~$24,047 restart), self-estimates; the restart ran on flat-rate plans. A Go-to-Rust TypeScript compiler port stalled near 84% after over $400,000 in tokens; a restart reports parity on upstream tests, with known gaps; unaudited.
- [GitHub moves its Copilot agent runtime from TypeScript to Rust using agents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-09-16-github-copilot-runtime-rust.md) — language, TypeScript on Node.js and V8 to Rust (native library with a C ABI); AI share: most; evidence: shown-in-source; author: seller-of-tool; cost: ~$120,000 for ~136.3 billion tokens (engineer time not priced). One engineer steered agent fleets to port about 430,000 lines of TypeScript to Rust in place, one component per PR, over 14.5 weeks.
- [Shopify rebuilds its React Native mobile apps natively for iOS and Android](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-09-10-shopify-react-native-to-native.md) — language, React Native apps (Shop first; Shopify, Point of Sale, Inbox to follow) to native iOS (Swift, SwiftUI) and Android (Kotlin, Jetpack Compose) apps; AI share: unstated; evidence: assertion-only; author: user-of-tool; cost: unstated. Agents port Shopify's React Native apps to native iOS and Android in gated checkpoints; the author says one-shot ports fail. The Shop app shipped in 12 weeks.
- [Temporal moves its Cloud billing store to ClickHouse with coding agents doing most of the cleanup](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-09-02-temporal-billing-store-clickhouse.md) — data, previous data warehouse (not named) behind the usage and billing tables to ClickHouse (ClickHouse Cloud); AI share: unstated; evidence: assertion-only; author: user-of-tool; cost: unstated. Saved agent prompts cover most deleted code and little new code; a shadow comparison caught an overflow, and agent instructions went stale.
- [Checkly rewrites its Node.js results daemon in Go with Claude Code](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-09-01-checkly-nodejs-to-go.md) — language, Node.js background worker in plain JavaScript (Results Daemon) to Go service; AI share: most; evidence: assertion-only; author: user-of-tool; cost: the accepted agent run fit in one day's token allowance of a $200 plan; the discarded run and people's time are not costed. A black-box harness with golden files from the legacy daemon judged an overnight agent rewrite in Go; its simplified queue model broke retries.
- [Intel's IDEAS harness ports the libgit2 command-line client in C to safe Rust](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-08-24-intel-ideas-c-to-rust.md) — language, C (libgit2 command-line client) to safe Rust (no unsafe code); AI share: most; evidence: shown-in-source; author: seller-of-tool; cost: ~$0.55 per symbol for translation (total unstated), plus ~$6.5 for repair. An LLM harness turned 112K lines of C into safe Rust that compiled but crashed; 8 person-hours guiding an agent got git blame working.
- [Asana finishes its Enzyme to React Testing Library move with Codex agents in two weeks](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-08-07-asana-enzyme-to-rtl.md) — test-framework, Enzyme (frontend React tests) to React Testing Library; AI share: unstated; evidence: assertion-only; author: seller-of-tool; cost: ~$11,000 model usage plus ~$1,000 infrastructure. Up to 4 Codex agents on a 5-sentence prompt removed Enzyme in about 1.5 weeks of engineering time for about $12K; stale docs and slow lint got in the way.
- [Bun moves its JavaScript runtime off Zig onto Rust with Claude agents in 11 days](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-07-08-bun-zig-to-rust.md) — language, Zig (Bun runtime, bundler, package manager, test runner) to Rust (about 100 crates); AI share: most; evidence: shown-in-source; author: seller-of-tool; cost: ~$165,000 at API list prices for the tokens used before merge (690 million output tokens, 5.9 billion fresh input tokens, 72 billion cached input tokens). One engineer ran about 50 Claude Code workflows, up to 64 agents at once, to port 535K lines of Zig to Rust in 11 days; 19 known regressions, all fixed.
- [GitLab uses AI agents to move its application rate limiter onto a shared Ruby gem](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-07-08-gitlab-rate-limiting.md) — architecture, Gitlab::ApplicationRateLimiter in the GitLab monolith (a Rack-level limiter moves next) to a single implementation in the labkit-ruby gem; AI share: unstated; evidence: assertion-only; author: seller-of-tool; cost: unstated. Agents moved 121 rate-limit keys onto one gem; 17 keys slipped past the plan, and a divergence that shadow mode had flagged still reached users.
- [Mindstone folds 86 Go targets into one TypeScript monolith with coding agents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-07-06-mindstone-go-to-typescript.md) — mixed, 86 Go targets (55 microservices plus crons, webhooks, GraphQL edges, libraries, APIs; RPC, Kafka, ScyllaDB, Redis on Kubernetes) to a single TypeScript service running on Cloud Run (Hono, graphql-yoga, Node 24); AI share: most; evidence: assertion-only; author: user-of-tool; cost: unstated. Agents rewrote 86 Go targets as one TypeScript service in about 2 weeks, checked by tests run on both: the first suite chased coverage, asserting nothing.
- [Datadog moves Stream Router storage off FoundationDB onto PostgreSQL and DuckDB](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-06-23-datadog-foundationdb-to-postgres.md) — data, FoundationDB key-value store (write path) and RocksDB snapshots (read path) to relational schema on PostgreSQL (write path) and DuckDB snapshots (read path); AI share: most; evidence: assertion-only; author: user-of-tool; cost: unstated. People redesigned a key-value store as a relational schema; Claude and Cursor ported the storage methods one failing test at a time.
- [1Password uses AI agents to refactor its Go monolith and begin a service extraction](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-04-20-1password-monolith-refactor.md) — architecture, Go monolith (B5), database transactions opened with MustBegin (panics on failure) to separately owned services; transaction calls that return errors; AI share: unstated; evidence: assertion-only; author: user-of-tool; cost: unstated. Agents rewrote over 3,000 panicking transaction calls from a tight spec, but stumbled on a service extraction's ordering and invariants.
- [Lutz Leonhardt starts moving 44 Angular form components in a Spartacus fork to Signal Forms](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-04-13-lutz-leonhardt-spartacus-signal-forms.md) — framework, Angular Reactive Forms (FormBuilder, Validators) to Angular Signal Forms through SignalFormControl, the interop first stage; AI share: most; evidence: shown-in-source; author: user-of-tool; cost: unstated. Claude Code sub-agents in worktrees moved Angular forms to Signal Forms, 34 of 44 marked done; a review found untested successes and silent rule changes.
- [PagerDuty's product manager gets Rundeck's Grails 7 upgrade to 99.7% passing tests in 9 days](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-04-13-pagerduty-rundeck-grails-7.md) — framework, Rundeck on Grails 6 (Spring Boot 2.7, Spring Security 5, Hibernate 5, Groovy 3, Java 11, javax) to Rundeck on Grails 7 (Spring Boot 3.2, Spring Security 6, Hibernate 6, Groovy 4, Java 17, jakarta); AI share: unstated; evidence: assertion-only; author: user-of-tool; cost: $200 in AI tools. A product manager with Claude Sonnet 4.5 in Cursor took Rundeck to Grails 7 in 9 days before engineer review; a Groovy 4 equals() change dropped the admin role.
- [Uber moves 75K test classes off JUnit 4 onto JUnit 5 with OpenRewrite; an AI attempt failed](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-04-07-uber-junit4-to-junit5.md) — test-framework, Java tests on JUnit 4 in a Bazel monorepo to Java tests on JUnit 5 (Jupiter engine on the JUnit Platform); AI share: little; evidence: assertion-only; author: user-of-tool; cost: unstated. Contrast case. Rule-based OpenRewrite recipes moved over 75,000 Java test classes onto JUnit 5; a generative-AI attempt failed and AI only helped debug.
- [Ladybird ports its JavaScript engine front end from C++ to Rust with Claude Code and Codex](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-02-23-ladybird-libjs-rust.md) — language, C++ (LibJS lexer, parser, AST, scope analysis and bytecode generator) to Rust (one crate linked into LibJS through a C interface); AI share: most; evidence: assertion-only; author: user-of-tool; cost: unstated. One engineer steered Claude Code and Codex to port LibJS's lexer, parser and bytecode generator to Rust in about 2 weeks, with identical output to C++.
- [Christopher Chedeau moves the Pokémon Showdown battle engine off TypeScript onto Rust with Claude Code](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-01-25-vjeux-pokemon-showdown-rust.md) — language, Pokémon Showdown battle engine (TypeScript; the post calls it JavaScript) to Rust; AI share: most; evidence: shown-in-source; author: user-of-tool; cost: unstated. One engineer had Claude Code write about 100k lines of Rust in a month, checked against the original on millions of seeded battles; no Rust written by hand.
- [Spotify runs fleet-wide migrations with its Honk background coding agent](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-11-06-spotify-honk.md) — mixed, many (for example Java AutoValue classes, old Scio versions, deprecated datasets) to many (for example Java records, the newest Scio, new dataset versions); AI share: most; evidence: assertion-only; author: seller-of-tool; cost: unstated. Spotify put a coding agent inside its fleet migration tooling; verifiers and an LLM judge gate each PR, and over 1,500 agent PRs were merged.
- [Robert Marshall moves his Gatsby blog to Next.js with Claude Code, after a failed first run](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-08-09-robert-marshall-gatsby-to-nextjs.md) — framework, Gatsby (blog fed by headless WordPress) to Next.js App Router; AI share: unstated; evidence: assertion-only; author: user-of-tool; cost: unstated. A one-prompt sub-agent migration rebuilt Gatsby's data layers inside Next.js; a restart from a fresh Next.js app, moving parts one at a time, worked.
- [Google widens int32 IDs to int64 in 39 migrations with an LLM pipeline](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-04-13-google-int64-ids.md) — data, int32 ID fields in protocol buffer schemas and the code using them (Java, C++, Dart and others) to int64 ID fields; AI share: most; evidence: shown-in-source; author: seller-of-tool; cost: unstated. A nightly pipeline of code search, rule-based sorting, an internal Gemini model and staged checks drafted 74.45% of 595 code changes in 39 ID migrations.
- [Airbnb moves 3.5K React test files off Enzyme onto React Testing Library](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-04-01-airbnb-enzyme-to-rtl.md) — test-framework, Enzyme (React component tests) to React Testing Library; AI share: most; evidence: assertion-only; author: user-of-tool; cost: unstated. An LLM pipeline with per-file validation steps and retries migrated 97% of about 3,500 React test files; people finished the rest by hand.
- [Zalando moves partner apps from one in-house UI component library to another with GPT-4o](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-02-20-zalando-ui-component-libraries.md) — framework, in-house UI component library (React) to another in-house UI component library (React); AI share: part; evidence: assertion-only; author: user-of-tool; cost: under $40 per repository in GPT-4o API fees (estimate). A Python tool fed GPT-4o hand-checked mappings and examples per component group; over 90% of migrated lines were right, and one bad change reached production.
- [Slack pairs a syntax-tree codemod with Claude 2.1 to help move 15K Enzyme tests to React Testing Library](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2024-05-22-slack-enzyme-to-rtl.md) — test-framework, Enzyme (React unit and integration tests) to React Testing Library; AI share: unstated; evidence: shown-in-source; author: user-of-tool; cost: unstated. Codemod alone 45% (evaluation files), Claude 2.1 alone 40-60% (base not given), both 80% of code in 9 checked files; 22% of tests passed over 338 files.

## Before you migrate: checklist

Questions to measure on a repository before an AI-driven move to another language, framework or
library, or a large restructuring. It guides an agent through what the cases show; it does not
decide for the project: findings and options go to the project's owner, who chooses. Each question
has a **Check**, what to measure and report (a measurement, not a verdict), the **Lessons** behind
it (`TST-2`: lesson 2 on the testing page; listed in [lessons/evidence.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/evidence.md)) and
a **Guide**, `guide/q<n>.md`, read only for the question in use: those lessons in our words with
links to them and their cases, what the question looks like in a project, questions to ask of this
one, the trade-offs, and when not to apply it. A threshold or hard rule carries a marker such as
(P3): the [Provenance](#provenance) table gives its source, evidence level, what it prevents and how
it fails applied blindly. `ours` and "(ours)" mark the maintainer's reading or a number we picked:
adapt it. A revisit reads [corrections.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/corrections.md) first.

1. **Is the move allowed, possible and worth it?**
   Check: find the written reason and the measured problem behind it (none written: ask the
   owner); repository rules that pin the stack, forbid new libraries or name an approver (one
   that forbids the target is the first finding the owner weighs (P1)); for each framework the
   product rests on (renderer, UI, desktop shell, platform or store SDK), its mature equivalent in
   the target, or mark the move a rewrite on a new base; where time, memory or money goes today
   (a profile, a bill) and whether the code to port is on that path; who maintains the result and
   whether they read the target language; what the target must win, as numbers where possible.
   Lessons: PLN-7, PLN-8, PLN-9, SEC-7.
   Guide: [guide/q1.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/guide/q1.md).
2. **Is there a test oracle that survives the move and that the agent cannot edit?**
   Check: count the tests that exercise behaviour through a public interface (CLI, API, files
   written, a headless harness) apart from white-box tests; list public features with none; run
   them once and list those that fail or will not run. Find golden files tied to the old
   implementation and how they are regenerated. Say how results are compared across languages
   (plain-data summaries, tolerances) and how you confirm the tests ran. When the tests are what
   moves, say how intent and coverage are compared (coverage before and after, a hand-converted
   sample) and check new tests can fail. Say whether old and new can run the same inputs side by
   side, outputs compared (a differential or shadow run), and how late a wrong
   change first fails (build, tests, or only once deployed). Find who must approve a test change
   (CODEOWNERS, branch rules, CI, the owner); none is a finding.
   Lessons: TST-1, TST-2, TST-3, TST-4, TST-5, TST-6, TST-8, TST-10, TST-12, TST-13, TST-14, TST-15,
   VER-5, VER-11, OVS-1.
   Guide: [guide/q2.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/guide/q2.md).
3. **Can an agent build, check and test alone, fast, and in parallel, in both toolchains?**
   Check: find the command that builds, formats, lints and tests one unit in the old stack, and
   name the one for the target stack (say whether its toolchain is pinned). Use recorded timings first (logs, CI
   history); otherwise time each, count the output lines of a failure, and build and test two
   fresh clones outside the repository at once as an agent would (install dependencies, count
   the tests that ran, cap the time; not worktrees, which write into the measured repository's
   `.git`) (P2). For the agents you plan, estimate compile time, disk space and speed, and process
   limits; say how agents are kept from undoing each other's work, and which target platforms
   their machines can build and test; for an app, how an agent drives it and how long one test
   takes. A missing formatter or linter is a finding.
   Lessons: OPS-1, OPS-2, OPS-3, ORC-1, ORC-2, VER-2, VER-4, TOL-6, TOL-8.
   Guide: [guide/q3.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/guide/q3.md).
4. **How big is the job, really?**
   Check: scope is everything that must exist in the target. Count lines and files in scope by
   folder (`scc`, `tokei`, `cloc`, else `git ls-files -z -- <scope> | xargs -0 wc -l`) for
   code (GPU too), tests, build scripts, and other languages (shaders, generated files,
   templates or DSLs of the old stack). For a change across call sites, list every site with a
   code index or static analyzer, not text search alone, and keep the list. Add code tangled with
   the scope. List the data and asset formats both builds read, and stored data that must stay
   readable (rows, hashes, saves). Give the change rate in scope over the last quarter
   (`git log --since="3 months ago" --numstat --format=%ad --date=short -- <scope>`): commits and
   lines per week, active days, last change. Code still changing fast: ask the owner whether to
   wait, or delete the old code in the change that ports it so later edits conflict (P3).
   Lessons: PLN-3, PLN-10, ROL-4, TOL-1, TOL-3, MSR-8.
   Guide: [guide/q4.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/guide/q4.md).
5. **Can the work ship in small units, with old and new side by side?**
   Check: split the scope into units (files, components, packages, repositories), draw their
   dependency order with a read-only graph tool for the language (`go mod graph`, `cargo tree`,
   `jdeps`, `madge`, `pydeps`), and count the cycles (Go and Cargo reject package cycles: look
   between modules or files instead), and mark the leaves that touch neither I/O nor shared
   state. Find the seam that lets one unit switch while the rest stays, and how the build links
   both languages meanwhile (seams by kind of move: [pitfalls.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/pitfalls.md#seams)). No seam:
   say so, the move is one switch. Check what the platform rules allow. Propose pilot units.
   Lessons: PLN-1, PLN-4, PLN-11, ROL-1, ROL-6, ORC-4.
   Guide: [guide/q5.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/guide/q5.md).
6. **Is the end state written, and is the scope held?**
   Check: look for a written target for the whole migration (not one unit), before-and-after
   examples from this repository, sites grouped into patterns with a template each, when the
   agent must stop and escalate, a rule to translate first and redesign later, and a check on
   each diff for changes outside its scope (P4). A repository rule against translating first (delete
   old paths, keep no compatibility) is a finding (P5).
   Lessons: CTX-4, PLN-2, PLN-5, PLN-13, REV-4, AGF-2, AGF-4.
   Guide: [guide/q6.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/guide/q6.md).
7. **What does the old stack do implicitly?**
   Check: search the scope for behaviour the target will not give for free, with the lists for
   this kind of move in [pitfalls.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/pitfalls.md) as it says. Make a table of direct dependencies: target
   library, version, stable release or archived (a missing framework is question 1).
   Lessons: REV-3, OPS-4, TST-7, VER-6, SEC-5, SEC-6, AGF-3, SEC-10.
   Guide: [guide/q7.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/guide/q7.md).
8. **Is the code uniform enough for one prompt, and what context goes with it?**
   Check: group the units by kind of code (pure logic, concurrency, OS layer, GPU or UI, data
   pipelines) and by framework, build system and style. For each group, name the context an
   agent gets: the unit's source, its neighbours' tests, good examples, mapping tables for
   renamed fields or APIs, runtime facts a person would look at, and what a rule-based codemod
   can do first. Say whether the model was piloted on the hardest files of each language in scope (else propose a pilot), and check the
   largest files fit its context window. A group too varied for one prompt is a candidate to defer
   or do by hand. Search docs and agent instructions for advice favouring the old stack.
   Lessons: CTX-1, CTX-2, CTX-3, CTX-5, CTX-9, CTX-10, CTX-11, CTX-12, CTX-13, TOL-2, TOL-7, TOL-9,
   AGF-8, PLN-8, PLN-12.
   Guide: [guide/q8.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/guide/q8.md).
9. **How will you work the long tail, stop, and learn from failures?**
   Check: look for a status record per unit, a way to rerun failing units by step, a retry limit
   (for independent units such as files; where units depend on each other, a rule to fix the
   workflow and rerun instead), a rule for when to stop automating and finish by hand, and a place
   where a failure seen twice becomes a standing instruction, skill or eval (P6).
   Lessons: VER-3, KNW-1, KNW-2, KNW-4, KNW-5, OVS-3, OVS-5, CTX-7, AGF-7, OPS-6, ROL-8, TST-11.
   Guide: [guide/q9.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/guide/q9.md).
10. **What may the agent decide and reach alone, and who reviews?**
    Check: list the guardrails an agent could switch off (deleting or editing tests, updating
    snapshots or baselines, waiver labels, CI flags) and who must approve each; the steps kept
    for people (schema changes, backfills, deploy order); and the tools, skills and credentials
    agent sessions can reach. A rule only written down, with nothing enforcing it, is a
    finding: say what could enforce it, if the owner wants it enforced. Changes in other teams' code: count the owning teams,
    whether they asked for the move, who carries the deploy risk. Ask the owner who reviews,
    whether they read the target language, and their hours a week.
    Lessons: OVS-1, OVS-2, AGF-1, AGF-5, AGF-9, SEC-1, SEC-2, SEC-3, REV-1, REV-2, REV-9, REV-11,
    TEM-4, TEM-6, ROL-9.
    Guide: [guide/q10.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/guide/q10.md).
11. **How will changes reach users?**
    Check: find the release channels (pre-release, flags, canary), the share of users each
    reaches, how problems are reported and watched, and how one unit's change is rolled back (for
    a single-user or internal tool: what a release and a rollback are). Not released yet: mark it
    "not applicable yet" and say what must exist before the first release.
    Lessons: ROL-2, ROL-3, ROL-5, ROL-7, ROL-10, ROL-11, VER-1, OPS-5, OPS-8.
    Guide: [guide/q11.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/guide/q11.md).
12. **How will you measure cost and result?**
    Check: write down the manual estimate and how it was made. Measure, before the port and on
    fixed hardware, the number the product exists for (speed, latency, memory, output quality),
    and the part the port changes, if not the same path. Plan to record tokens or spend, engineer
    hours, pull requests, regressions after merge and reverts, marking measured against estimated.
    Lessons: CST-1, CST-2, CST-6, CST-7, MSR-1, MSR-2, MSR-4, MSR-5, MSR-9, MSR-10, TST-9, KNW-3.
    Guide: [guide/q12.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/guide/q12.md).

### Starting thresholds

Numbers from one case each: points of comparison, not targets. Where a question has none, its
Check's measurement stands on its own.

- Q4: GitHub first counted about 130,000 lines; about 430,000 went through the port (P7). A scope
  count with no allowance for code moving in or newly written is a finding to report (P7).
  [GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-09-16-github-copilot-runtime-rust.md)
- Q5: Bun ran its whole loop on 3 files before all 1,448 (P8). No pilot before the bulk run is a
  finding to report (P8). [Bun](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-07-08-bun-zig-to-rust.md)
- Q9: most of Airbnb's simple and medium files passed within about 10 attempts; 50 to 100
  attempts on the hardest gained little (P9). In a bulk run of many units, no retry limit, or no
  rule to stop and hand-port, is a finding to report (P9). [Airbnb](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-04-01-airbnb-enzyme-to-rtl.md)

### How to run this checklist

1. Run it in a fresh session on the repository to migrate, changing nothing there (P10). Look for
   the record `docs/migration-review.md` first: with none, this is the first review, up to step 9;
   with one, a revisit (step 10). Say in one line which and why, the report's "Path:" line. The
   cases are few and mostly their teams' own accounts: read "What went wrong" before relying on them.
2. Measure first: answer each Check with a number, file or command output, not from memory.
3. A check you may not run: write the exact command, mark it "not run" with the reason, never
   guess its result (P11). Logs or CI history count if you name their source.
4. A fact only the owner knows (review time, budget): write the question, mark it "ask the
   owner" and state a default; unanswered, assume it, note it in the record, go on. A decision only
   the owner can make (approval of a new stack, a change to a project rule) is not assumed: it stays
   "waiting on the owner".
5. Report each question as a finding: what the Check found and did not find, with the
   measurement; or "nothing missing", or "not applicable yet" with what must exist first. A finding
   is a measurement for the owner to weigh, not a verdict; a Check part that does not fit the
   project's size or kind of move, as its guide's "When not to apply it" says, is reported as such.
6. Before writing a finding up, read the question's guide. Where its "When not to apply it" fits
   this project, say so: it may be the reason to leave things as they are. Build the options on
   the guide and, if you can, the cited lessons (their "Against" lines and oracle tags) and the case
   sections they link, above all "Practices to copy". Compare numbers across cases only in matching
   units. Keep the two readings apart: "(ours)" in the collection is the maintainer's, and so is a
   lesson tagged `[ours]`; label your own "agent's reading".
7. Give each finding options for the owner, each with its trade-off; leaving it as it is is often
   one. You may say which option the measurements favour and why, labelled "agent's reading". Order
   the findings so the owner meets first what the rest depend on: a project rule against the move
   (question 1), then the oracle, the baseline and the end state.
8. Report as below and wait for the owner's choice (P10): for each finding, do (which option),
   later or skip is theirs. One change per option (or parts 3a, 3b).
9. Apply and record, once the owner has chosen (P10) ("Apply what you recommended": the options your
   reading favoured, the rest later; "Apply 1A and 3B; 2 later; skip 5"; "Apply none; write the
   record"). In a read-only run, write no file (P10); show the record after the report. Else:
   - Write `docs/migration-review.md` in the measured repository (the one file this checklist adds
     there; format below) before changing anything, with each chosen proposal's baseline: how
     often its problem has happened so far, with the evidence. Complete it with every finding,
     the later and skipped ones too, the corrections.md entries checked ("none listed" if it has
     none) and the newest log.md entry this review covered.
   - Each row waiting for first use gets the owner (who looks for its event) and check-by date the
     owner named, or ones you propose for the owner to confirm. A question of fact left
     unanswered: assume the report's default and record the assumption; a decision left open (an
     approval, a change to a project rule) stays open.
   - Do the work the way this project normally runs work (yourself, or by briefing workers), one
     proposal at a time, on a branch. First state its "Check now" and its "Event that proves it";
     it is applied when the check now passes (waiting for first use), proven only once later work
     shows the event.
   - Stop at the first failing check (P12): leave that proposal open, its event naming the failed
     check, apply no later proposal, and report what failed and what is left. The owner decides.
10. Revisit: read [corrections.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/corrections.md) first, then go on as step 7 of
    [applying the lessons](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/docs/applying-lessons.md) says, with the questions its `changes/` files
    list as well as the lessons. Report in the revisit format; change nothing but the record (P10) until
    the owner chooses, then apply as in step 9.
11. Share (optional): a [field report](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/docs/field-reports.md) once an item has met its problem.

### Report format

The report, the revisit report and the record `docs/migration-review.md`: [docs/report-formats.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/docs/report-formats.md).

### Provenance

Levels: `published case` (one), `published cases` (two or more), `others' measurement`,
`vendor guidance`, `ours`.

| ID | Source | Level | Prevents | Blind failure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| P1 | ours | ours | a port planned against the project's own rules without the owner seeing it | holding the move where the rule only asks for an approver |
| P2 | clones: OPS-1, ORC-1; no worktree, time cap: ours | ours | a measurement that hangs or writes into the measured repository | refusing worktrees for the port itself, where they kept agents apart |
| P3 | [GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-09-16-github-copilot-runtime-rust.md), ROL-4 | published case | edits to old code after its port | deleting old code a side-by-side run (Q2) or a rollback (Q11) still needs |
| P4 | CTX-4, AGF-2, REV-4 | published cases | agents guessing past what they understand; diffs straying from the task | a stop rule so wide that every unit waits for a person |
| P5 | PLN-5 | published cases | a redesign inside the port, so a failure points nowhere | flagging a redesign the owner chose (PLN-5's Against lists moves that built the target first) |
| P6 | VER-3, OVS-3, KNW-1 | published cases | endless retries; one failure fixed by hand again and again | a retry cap on units judged independent that share state |
| P7 | [GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-09-16-github-copilot-runtime-rust.md), PLN-3 | published case | a plan sized on the first count | taking threefold growth as a rule for every project |
| P8 | [Bun](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-07-08-bun-zig-to-rust.md), PLN-1 | published case | a bulk run on an untried loop | taking three files as pilot enough for code of several kinds (Q8) |
| P9 | [Airbnb](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-04-01-airbnb-enzyme-to-rtl.md), VER-3 | published case | attempts spent on files that will not pass | ten attempts as a cap for units that are not small independent files |
| P10 | ours | ours | changes the owner did not choose | skipping read-only builds and tests, or no record after the owner chose |
| P11 | ours | ours | invented measurements | marking checks "not run" that could run safely |
| P12 | ours | ours | later changes piled on a failed one, so the failure points nowhere | stopping for a check that failed before the change too; report that, and let the owner decide |

[GitHub]: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-09-16-github-copilot-runtime-rust.md
[Bun]: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-07-08-bun-zig-to-rust.md
[Airbnb]: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-04-01-airbnb-enzyme-to-rtl.md

## Q1 guide: Is the move allowed, possible and worth it?

For question 1 of the [checklist](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/checklist.md): read it before writing up a finding on that
question. It walks through what the cases show; the project's owner decides. Each point names its
evidence: a lesson ID (its strength, its cases and the cases against it are in
[lessons/evidence.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/evidence.md); its page links the case sections) or a case link.
"(ours)" marks the maintainer's reading, evidence level `ours`; so does a lesson tagged `[ours]` there,
which is our inference from its cases.

### Lessons behind it

- [PLN-7](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/planning.md): agents lower the price of a rewrite once shelved for cost, but
  the fair comparison is with doing nothing, not with a manual rewrite nobody would have funded.
- [PLN-8](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/planning.md): parts that cannot be specified or checked (an unsupported
  platform, a language the model handles poorly) were left out rather than forced.
- [PLN-9](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/planning.md): the published cases are success stories, so the odds they
  suggest run high; a partial outcome and a way to stop belong in the plan.
- [SEC-7](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/security.md): each library the move replaces is a small migration of its
  own, above all security-sensitive ones.

Cases, in our words: the cases start from a known problem or forced move (GitHub's startup and
memory, Bun's crashes, Slack's blocked React upgrade, Google's int32 limit). The rest is ours.

### What it looks like in a project

- A written reason ties the move to a measured problem: a profile, a bill, a crash count, a
  limit about to be reached ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-09-16-github-copilot-runtime-rust.md#what-was-migrated), [Google](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-04-13-google-int64-ids.md#what-was-migrated)).
- The product rests on a framework (a renderer, a desktop shell, a store SDK) with no mature
  equivalent in the target, so the move is a rewrite on a new base rather than a port (ours).
- The repository's own rules pin the stack, forbid new libraries or name an approver; such a rule
  shapes the move before any measurement does (ours).

### Questions to ask of this project

- What problem does the move solve, and where is it measured?
- Is the code to port on the path where the time, memory or money goes?
- Which rule of the project's own speaks to the move: one that forbids the target, or one that
  only asks for an approver?
- Who maintains the result, and do they read the target language?
- What must the target win, in numbers, for the move to have been worth it?

### Trade-offs

- Moving for a measured problem gives a test of success; moving for fashion gives none, but a
  forced move (an end-of-life framework) may have no number and still be needed (PLN-7).
- A rewrite on a new base can fix design debt the port would carry over, at the price of losing
  the old code as the reference (PLN-5, PLN-13).
- Porting without the code's owners close to it saves their time now; in one case it made debugging
  and incident handling harder later, and other cases disagree (TEM-5).

### When not to apply it

- A rule that only names an approver is a question for that person, not a reason to hold the move
  (ours).
- When the owner has already decided to move for reasons outside the code (hiring, a vendor's end
  of support), the "worth it" part informs the plan rather than the decision (ours).

## Q2 guide: Is there a test oracle that survives the move and that the agent cannot edit?

For question 2 of the [checklist](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/checklist.md): read it before writing up a finding on that
question. It walks through what the cases show; the project's owner decides. Each point names its
evidence: a lesson ID (its strength, its cases and the cases against it are in
[lessons/evidence.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/evidence.md); its page links the case sections) or a case link.
"(ours)" marks the maintainer's reading, evidence level `ours`; so does a lesson tagged `[ours]` there,
which is our inference from its cases.

### Lessons behind it

- [TST-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/testing.md): a black-box suite that does not depend on the language judged
  the port, run against old and new.
- [TST-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/testing.md): the missing-feature regressions came from behaviour no test
  covered.
- [TST-3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/testing.md): matching the old system does not make the port right; a
  faithful port carries the old bugs.
- [TST-4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/testing.md): checks compiled only into debug builds hid release-build
  regressions.
- [TST-5](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/testing.md): where tests were thin, recorded inputs and outputs of the old
  system stood in.
- [TST-6](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/testing.md): a red baseline or golden files that cannot be regenerated stall
  correct changes.
- [TST-8](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/testing.md): when tests are what moves, passing proves little; counts,
  coverage and intent need comparing.
- [TST-10](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/testing.md): one generation writing both code and tests invites tests that
  cannot fail.
- [TST-12](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/testing.md), [TST-13](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/testing.md): old and new compared on what
  users and other systems see, side by side on the same inputs.
- [TST-14](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/testing.md): coverage rose while agent-written tests asserted nothing.
- [TST-15](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/testing.md): a harness simpler than production let a production bug through.
- [VER-5](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/verification.md): a green run can hide tests that never ran.
- [VER-11](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/verification.md): how late a wrong change first fails shapes the pipeline.
- [OVS-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/oversight.md): the agent that changes code should not change what counts as
  correct.

Cases, in our words: GitHub's unchanged end-to-end suites were the oracle; its feature-loss
regressions came almost all from their gaps. Bun's suite, in a third language, judged the whole
port (a critic notes it missed the old bugs). Google's correct changes stalled on failing tests
and goldens; Spotify's worst case is green CI with wrong behaviour. Intel, Shopify, ts-rust,
Pokémon and Ladybird ran old and new on the same inputs (Ladybird also edited its expected outputs
in that change). Bloomberg's changes could fail only once deployed; Checkly's harness passed while
production retries failed.

### What it looks like in a project

- Tests that drive the product from outside (a CLI, an API, files written) survive a language
  change; unit tests tied to the old code's internals usually do not, unless they are ported too ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-09-16-github-copilot-runtime-rust.md#how-it-was-checked), [Bun](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-07-08-bun-zig-to-rust.md#how-it-was-checked)).
- Golden files and snapshots that only the old implementation can regenerate (TST-6).
- A suite that is green while some tests are skipped or never collected (VER-5).
- No rule on who may edit a test: the agent can make a failing check pass by changing it (OVS-1,
  AGF-5).

### Questions to ask of this project

- Which public features have no test that drives them from outside?
- Which tests fail or will not run today, before any change?
- Can old and new run the same inputs, with outputs compared, and what varies per run?
- How late does a wrong change first fail here: at build, in tests, or only once deployed?
- Who must approve a change to a test, a snapshot or a baseline, and what enforces it?

### Trade-offs

- An outside suite is slow to build where none exists; recorded inputs and outputs are quicker but
  freeze the old bugs as expected behaviour (TST-3, TST-5).
- Locking tests against agent edits protects the oracle and slows legitimate test fixes, which
  then sit until a person approves them (OVS-1).
- A side-by-side run catches what tests miss, at the cost of making the old output deterministic
  first (TST-13).

### When not to apply it

- When the tests are what moves (a test-framework change), the suite cannot judge itself; compare
  counts and intent instead (TST-8).
- An owner who chose to fix known old bugs during the move gives up exact equality with the old
  system on those paths, by design (TST-3, PLN-5).

## Q3 guide: Can an agent build, check and test alone, fast, and in parallel, in both toolchains?

For question 3 of the [checklist](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/checklist.md): read it before writing up a finding on that
question. It walks through what the cases show; the project's owner decides. Each point names its
evidence: a lesson ID (its strength, its cases and the cases against it are in
[lessons/evidence.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/evidence.md); its page links the case sections) or a case link.
"(ours)" marks the maintainer's reading, evidence level `ours`; so does a lesson tagged `[ours]` there,
which is our inference from its cases.

### Lessons behind it

- [OPS-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/operations.md): parallel agents saturated CPU, disk and I/O; one build at a
  time, through a lease, kept the machine usable.
- [OPS-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/operations.md): operating-system limits contained heavy tests; asking the
  agent to be careful did not.
- [OPS-3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/operations.md): agents spend their time reading, building and testing, so a
  fast inner loop comes before more agents.
- [ORC-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/orchestration.md): agents sharing one working copy wrecked each other's work.
- [ORC-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/orchestration.md): parallel agents only on changes that are independent by
  design.
- [VER-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/verification.md): cheap checks first, and a candidate dropped at its first
  failure.
- [VER-4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/verification.md): one verify tool that returns short errors.
- [TOL-6](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/tooling.md): formatters, linters and type checks inside the agent's loop.
- [TOL-8](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/tooling.md): a way to drive the running app directly, not through
  screenshots.

Cases, in our words: GitHub needed a build lock. Bun's agents sharing one checkout undid each
other's work within minutes, and heavy tests stalled the machine. 1Password and Spartacus gave
each agent a worktree (Spartacus's tests failed to start there); Spotify's verify tool returns
short errors. Shopify's agents took minutes per test in simulators; Asana's lint was slow and CI
disagreed with local runs.

### What it looks like in a project

- One command builds, lints and tests a unit, and its failure output is short enough to read in
  one go ([Spotify](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-11-06-spotify-honk.md#what-worked)).
- A test run that needs a running service, a simulator or a manual step the agent cannot do
  (TOL-8).
- Timings recorded in CI history, or none, so they must be measured from fresh clones (ours).
- Two agents building at once slow each other or fight over one checkout ([Bun](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-07-08-bun-zig-to-rust.md#what-went-wrong)).

### Questions to ask of this project

- What is the one command for one unit, in the old stack and in the target?
- How long does it take, and how many lines does a failure print?
- What happens when two fresh clones build and test at once on this machine?
- How are agents kept from undoing each other's work, and which platforms can their machines build?
- For an app: how does an agent drive it, and how long does one test take?

### Trade-offs

- A worktree per agent keeps agents apart cheaply, but some test setups fail to start in one; a
  full clone costs disk and install time (ORC-1).
- A build lease keeps the machine usable at the price of agents waiting their turn (OPS-1).
- Making the inner loop faster first delays the port and pays back on every later run (OPS-3).

### When not to apply it

- A single agent working alone needs no parallel measurement; the timing of one unit still
  matters (ours).
- Worktrees are only ruled out for measuring the repository, since they write into its `.git`;
  for the port itself they kept agents apart (ORC-1).

## Q4 guide: How big is the job, really?

For question 4 of the [checklist](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/checklist.md): read it before writing up a finding on that
question. It walks through what the cases show; the project's owner decides. Each point names its
evidence: a lesson ID (its strength, its cases and the cases against it are in
[lessons/evidence.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/evidence.md); its page links the case sections) or a case link.
"(ours)" marks the maintainer's reading, evidence level `ours`; so does a lesson tagged `[ours]` there,
which is our inference from its cases.

### Lessons behind it

- [PLN-3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/planning.md): in a live repository, scope grew while the work ran, as code
  moved in and new code was written.
- [PLN-10](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/planning.md): counting how often each pattern is used showed which
  transforms paid back first.
- [ROL-4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/rollout.md): deleting the old code in the change that adds the new turned
  concurrent edits into conflicts instead of silent losses.
- [TOL-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/tooling.md): deterministic tools (analysers, call-site lists) built and
  reviewed first, then agents bound to them.
- [TOL-3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/tooling.md): change sites found with a code index or static analysis, erring
  on too many.
- [MSR-8](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/measurement.md): finding the sites was often the hard part, done by tools,
  not the model.

Cases, in our words: GitHub's scope grew about threefold as code moved in and the old code kept
growing. Google's code index beat text search but listed irrelevant sites; 1Password's analyzer
listed every site.

### What it looks like in a project

- Code outside the folder being moved (shared helpers, generated files, templates, shaders) that
  must exist in the target too ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-09-16-github-copilot-runtime-rust.md#what-went-wrong)).
- A change across call sites whose list came from text search, which misses uses reached through
  other variables ([Google](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2025-04-13-google-int64-ids.md#what-went-wrong)).
- Code in scope still changing every week, so a port started now chases a moving target (PLN-3).
- Stored data (rows, hashes, saved files) the new build must keep reading (ours).

### Questions to ask of this project

- What must exist in the target that is not in the folder being moved?
- How were the call sites found, and is the list kept?
- How fast is the code in scope changing, and who is changing it?
- Which data formats and stored data must stay readable across the move?

### Trade-offs

- Waiting for the code to settle avoids chasing edits but delays the move; deleting old code in the
  porting change surfaces edits as conflicts, but takes away what a side-by-side run or a rollback
  may still need (ROL-4; row P3 of the checklist's Provenance table).
- A static analyzer lists every site and some irrelevant ones; text search is quicker and misses
  indirect uses (TOL-3).

### When not to apply it

- Where old and new must run side by side (question 2's differential run, question 11's
  rollback), deleting the old code in the porting change takes away what they run on (ROL-4).
- A fixed file set with no inflow, like a test-framework move, gains little from re-measuring
  scope while the work runs (PLN-3).

## Q5 guide: Can the work ship in small units, with old and new side by side?

For question 5 of the [checklist](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/checklist.md): read it before writing up a finding on that
question. It walks through what the cases show; the project's owner decides. Each point names its
evidence: a lesson ID (its strength, its cases and the cases against it are in
[lessons/evidence.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/evidence.md); its page links the case sections) or a case link.
"(ours)" marks the maintainer's reading, evidence level `ours`; so does a lesson tagged `[ours]` there,
which is our inference from its cases.

### Lessons behind it

- [PLN-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/planning.md): the whole pipeline piloted on a few easy, well-tested units
  before the rest.
- [PLN-4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/planning.md): slices ordered along the dependency graph, leaves first, the hub
  last.
- [PLN-11](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/planning.md): one-pass ports of a whole app gave code nobody could maintain,
  in one author's account; others disagree.
- [ROL-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/rollout.md): one component swapped per change, old and new joined by a
  temporary bridge, so the main branch could always ship.
- [ROL-6](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/rollout.md): the size of the bridge as the progress signal.
- [ORC-4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/orchestration.md): the work queue built from deterministic output, then fanned
  out.

Cases, in our words: GitHub swapped one component per pull request through a temporary interop
layer, leaves first; Intel went in dependency order; Google, Airbnb and Spotify moved one ID, file
or repository at a time. Bun made one switch after a small trial, and cycles left by its package
split took two more agent runs. Shopify's author says one-pass ports give code that cannot ship;
small reviewed checkpoints replaced them. The cost of a mixed build is ours.

### What it looks like in a project

- A seam where one unit can switch while the rest stays: a component boundary, an ABI, a process,
  a route ([pitfalls.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/pitfalls.md#seams), ROL-1).
- Cycles between modules or files that keep any one of them from moving alone ([Bun](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-07-08-bun-zig-to-rust.md#what-went-wrong)).
- Leaves that touch neither I/O nor shared state, the cheap first units (PLN-4).
- No seam at all, so the move is one switch (ours).

### Questions to ask of this project

- What are the units, and in what dependency order do they fall?
- How many cycles, and where?
- Which seam lets one unit switch, and how does the build link both languages meanwhile?
- What do the platform rules allow (a store's review, a plugin host)?
- Which units make a pilot that runs the whole loop?

### Trade-offs

- A bridge between old and new keeps the main branch shippable and costs a mixed build to
  maintain until it reaches zero (ROL-1, ROL-6).
- One switch after a small trial is faster and saves the bridge, but every regression lands at
  once (Bun, in [PLN-11](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/planning.md)'s "Against").
- A pilot of a few units finds the loop's problems cheaply; it may miss problems that only appear
  at scale, such as agents clashing in one checkout (PLN-1).

### When not to apply it

- When the codebase has no seam and the owner accepts one switch, ordering units still helps the
  agents, though there are no small units to ship (ours).
- A pilot of a few easy files says little about code of several kinds; question 8 groups them
  (PLN-1, row P8 of the checklist's Provenance table).

## Q6 guide: Is the end state written, and is the scope held?

For question 6 of the [checklist](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/checklist.md): read it before writing up a finding on that
question. It walks through what the cases show; the project's owner decides. Each point names its
evidence: a lesson ID (its strength, its cases and the cases against it are in
[lessons/evidence.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/evidence.md); its page links the case sections) or a case link.
"(ours)" marks the maintainer's reading, evidence level `ours`; so does a lesson tagged `[ours]` there,
which is our inference from its cases.

### Lessons behind it

- [CTX-4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/context.md): a stated end state, its preconditions and when not to act; vague
  goals were read narrowly.
- [PLN-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/planning.md): most of the effort went into specs, guides and tooling before
  the bulk run.
- [PLN-5](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/planning.md): translate first, redesign later, so a failure points at the
  port; several moves built the target's design first and disagree.
- [PLN-13](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/planning.md): in a framework or data-store move, the target's foundation
  built first in its own idiom.
- [REV-4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/review.md): an automatic check comparing each diff with its instruction.
- [AGF-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/agent-failures.md): agents fill gaps in the spec with plausible guesses.
- [AGF-4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/agent-failures.md): agents stray beyond the task.

Cases, in our words: GitHub's agents ported only the hot paths until the full end state was
written, and each redesign allowed mid-port cost regressions, time or tokens. Bun wrote a porting
guide first and left idiomatic code for later. 1Password's call-site cleanup ran from a list,
templates and escalation rules; Spotify's judge rejects sessions mostly for straying from the
prompt. Two other moves built the target's design first.

### What it looks like in a project

- A written target for the whole migration, with before-and-after examples from this repository
  ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-09-16-github-copilot-runtime-rust.md#what-went-wrong), [Bun](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-07-08-bun-zig-to-rust.md#what-worked)).
- Sites grouped into patterns, each with a template, and named conditions under which the agent
  asks a person (CTX-4, AGF-2).
- A repository rule that pushes deletion over translation ("delete old paths, keep no
  compatibility"), which works against translating first (PLN-5).
- An owner's recorded decision to redesign during the move (PLN-13).

### Questions to ask of this project

- Where is the end state written, for the whole migration and not one unit?
- Which patterns do the sites fall into, and is there a template for each?
- Under which named conditions should the agent ask a person?
- Does the plan translate first, or redesign as it goes, and who chose that?
- What checks each diff for changes outside its task?

### Trade-offs

- Translating first makes each failure point at the port; redesigning during it can save a second
  pass but mixes two causes of change (PLN-5).
- A narrow escalation rule keeps agents moving; a wide one ("ask whenever unsure") holds every unit
  until a person answers (CTX-4, row P4 of the checklist's Provenance table).
- Writing the end state and templates first is slow and is where the effort went in the cases
  that report it (PLN-2).

### When not to apply it

- A redesign the owner chose is their decision; the finding is its cost (two causes of change in
  one diff) and how to keep each change checkable, not a call to undo it (PLN-5's "Against",
  PLN-13).
- A small, uniform move (one API across call sites) may need only a template and a scope check,
  not a full end-state document (ours).

## Q7 guide: What does the old stack do implicitly?

For question 7 of the [checklist](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/checklist.md): read it before writing up a finding on that
question. It walks through what the cases show; the project's owner decides. Each point names its
evidence: a lesson ID (its strength, its cases and the cases against it are in
[lessons/evidence.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/evidence.md); its page links the case sections) or a case link.
"(ours)" marks the maintainer's reading, evidence level `ours`; so does a lesson tagged `[ours]` there,
which is our inference from its cases.

### Lessons behind it

- [REV-3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/review.md): a written list of constructs that read alike in old and new code
  but behave differently, given to reviewers.
- [OPS-4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/operations.md): what the old runtime supplied silently, tested on every
  platform shipped.
- [TST-7](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/testing.md): values beyond the old range, at real data sizes, where numeric
  types or sums change.
- [VER-6](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/verification.md): machine-readable contracts so a changed interface fails
  mechanically.
- [SEC-5](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/security.md), [SEC-6](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/security.md): binding signatures generated by
  a tool; a bounds-checked target turns silent errors into crashes.
- [AGF-3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/agent-failures.md): agents handled order-dependent steps badly even when told.
- [SEC-10](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/lessons/security.md): the order of schema changes and backfills kept with people.

Cases, in our words: the regressions compiled: GitHub's runtime defaults and one-sided paired
operations, Bun's lines that read alike but behave differently, Intel's pointer comparison,
Google's bit operations and SQL tied to the old width, 1Password's backfill order, Zalando's wrong
data mapping that broke a live page, PagerDuty's equality change.

### What it looks like in a project

- Code that relies on defaults: a time zone, an environment read, a falsy check, a number type
  ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-09-16-github-copilot-runtime-rust.md#what-went-wrong)).
- Paired operations (open and close, subscribe and unsubscribe) where a port may carry one side
  only ([GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/cases/2026-09-16-github-copilot-runtime-rust.md#what-went-wrong)).
- Each item of the [pitfalls](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/ai-migrations/main/pitfalls.md) list for this kind of move, found in the scope by a
  search you can name (ours).
- A direct dependency whose target replacement is unmaintained or behaves differently (SEC-7).

### Questions to ask of this project

- Which items of the pitfalls list for this move appear in the scope, and by which search?
- Which direct dependencies have a stable equivalent in the target, and which are archived?
- Which orders (schema, writers, backfill) must hold across the switch, and who sets them?

### Trade-offs
